extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical philosophy (Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics), scholarly readers seeking commentary and explanatory notes
extracted.subtask_description: Explanatory notes and commentary on Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics (Books II–VI), clarifying Greek terms, distinctions, and normative claims about virtue, choice, and practical reasoning. Intended to guide interpretation and application of Aristotelian moral theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goods in esse vs in posse; faculties good only when rightly used
rubrics_metrics.description: An exhaustive division of goods: those in esse (in existence) are either above praise or subjects of praise; those in posse (here called faculties) are good only when rightly used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by examples: Rhetoric is a faculty which may be used to promote justice or abused to support villainy; money likewise — the goodness of a faculty depends on its right use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-control (enkrates) vs lack of self-control (akrates); formation of habits
rubrics_metrics.description: The enkrates is he who has bad or unruly appetites but whose reason is strong enough to keep them under; the akrates is he whose appetites constantly prevail over his reason and resolutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By the law of habits the enkrates approximates to sophrosyne (self-mastery) as remonstrances of reason grow stronger; the akrates' remonstrances grow fainter until silenced, producing akolasia. This account grounds moral assessment in habit-formation over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maturity of virtue measured by absence of pain
rubrics_metrics.description: No habit of courage or self-mastery can be said to be matured until pain altogether vanishes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The enkrates feels pain while restraining appetites; only with perfected self-mastery (sophrosyne) does the pain cease. Some fear is necessary to form true courage; permanence of virtue requires the eventual cessation of such painful struggle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue as due regulation of all parts of our nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue consists in the due regulation of all the parts of our nature; passions are real parts of that nature and have proper offices, so it is an error to aim at their extirpation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While a perfect moral state makes emotion rare, that state is attained by regular process (habituation). Aristotle favours cultivating passions to their right use rather than the Stoic eradication of passions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Praxis (process) vs pragma (result); habits form from actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Praxis denotes the whole process from conception to performance (action); pragma denotes only the result. No repetition of pragmata (results) goes to form a habit; habits are formed by repeating the process/actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A morally right outcome does not by itself create a virtuous habit if the process (praxis) was flawed. Example: a murderer killed by accomplices — the result might be 'right' but the praxis is not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral responsibility requires capacity, acts, and moral choice
rubrics_metrics.description: To make up the character of Justice (and more generally moral responsibility) men must have the capacity, do the acts, and do them from moral choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capacity (ability), the performance of relevant acts, and that those acts stem from deliberate moral choice are jointly required for full moral praise or blame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habituation: habits arise from repeated action in circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Habits being formed by acting in a certain way under certain circumstances, we can only choose how we will act, not what circumstances we will have to act under.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This grounds moral education: forming virtuous habits requires repeated right action in relevant contexts rather than mere theoretical assent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntariness and choice require deliberation and will
rubrics_metrics.description: The Will waits upon deliberation in which Reason is the judge; when the decision is pronounced, the Will must act accordingly. In purely compulsory cases there is no deliberation, decision, or will, and consequently no choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A voluntary action presupposes the sequence: wish → deliberation → decision → will → action. Compulsion truncates this sequence and removes moral responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage's necessary components: accurate danger appraisal and proper motive
rubrics_metrics.description: For true courage is required: 1) exact appreciation of danger; 2) a proper motive for resisting fear. Spurious kinds of courage fail in one or both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples contrast genuine bravery (properly motivated and accurately assessing risk) with cowardly or rash substitutes that lack one component.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actions, not opinions, form habits and constitute character
rubrics_metrics.description: On objects of moral choice, opinion is not the same as moral choice because actions alone form habits and constitute character; opinions are generally signs of character but when acted on they merge into moral choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotation used to illustrate: 'Treason doth never prosper, what's the reason? When it doth prosper, none dare call it Treason.' Meaning: acting on opinions transforms them into character-shaping choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish ignorance of facts vs ignorance of principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Any ignorance of particular facts affects the rightness not of the praxis (the action-process), but of the pragma (the result); ignorance of (i.e., incapacity to discern) principles shows the Moral Constitution to have been depraved—Conscience is perverted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral assessment must separate mistakes due to factual error from deeper failures of moral perception or principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motive (eneka) as designed causation; one cannot be ignorant of one's own motive
rubrics_metrics.description: Eneka denotes the relation of cause and effect as designed causation; used for Motive or final cause. It would be a contradiction to speak of a man being ignorant of his own Motive of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding actions requires recognizing their teleological aspect; examples (biblical) show acts that happen to produce effects cannot be mistaken for having had those effects as motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of no return in moral decline
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a certain bound to imprudence and misbehaviour which, being transgressed, there remains no place for repentance in the natural course of things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral declension can reach an irreversible stage—comparison with a stone set in motion and Bishop Butler's account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility connected to potential for moral improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: A man is not responsible for being 'theratos' (as formed by nature), because particular propensions must be felt; but he is responsible for being 'eutheratos' if he might have improved and raised himself to a higher state of virtue by contrary behaviour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral blame attaches when an agent had the capacity and opportunity to cultivate virtue but failed to do so; capacity to improve is a key condition for responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocation fairness requires proportion equality between persons and goods
rubrics_metrics.description: Before reciprocation is attempted, there must be the same ratio between the wares as between the persons, i.e., the ratio of equality; fairness in exchange depends on proportionality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated with examples (builder vs shoemaker) showing that unequal person-ratios require corresponding equality in goods exchanged to be fair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction's validity hinges on the mind performing it (subjective certainty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction is a branch of probable reasoning; its validity depends entirely upon the quality of the particular mind which performs it. Rapid induction is a distinguishing mark of genius and produces subjective, not objective, certainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Syllogistic presentations of induction are either nugatory or contain a literally false premiss; compare Aristotle's Analytica Prior/Post and Topics for fuller treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct logical division: membra dividentia must be opposed
rubrics_metrics.description: The test of correct logical division is that the membra dividentia shall be opposed, i.e., not included one by the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper definitions require coextensive and mutually exclusive partitions; this is the canon for logical classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual ends distinguish intellectual virtues (aplos vs eneka tinos)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mind attains truth either for the sake of truth itself (aplos) or for the sake of something further (eneka tinos). If for truth itself, by episteme, nous or sophia; if for something further, with a view to act (phronesis) or to make (techne).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different kinds of knowledge and practical reasoning correspond to different ends; this classification informs how we evaluate intellectual virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason should originate action though feelings may instigate it
rubrics_metrics.description: Reason ought to be the originator in all cases (as Conscience should be); nevertheless, a function of feelings and passions in our composite nature is to instigate action when Reason and Conscience by themselves do not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical moral psychology recognizes both ideal (reason-led) action and the empirical role of passions in motivating behavior; moral appraisal must account for this complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degrees of excellence: art vs practical wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: In strict sense Art (and Practical Wisdom) does not admit degrees of excellence; in popular language terms like 'wiser man' or 'better artist' denote different degrees of approximation to Practical Wisdom and Art respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious when attributing 'degrees' in technical senses—popular locutions may mask conceptual distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited stock of good implies zero-sum distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the stock of good is limited, if any individual takes more than his share some one else must have less than his share; where it is infinite or nonexistent this cannot happen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle underlies distributive justice analyses—finite goods create unavoidable trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical wisdom (phronesis) applies general principles; domain-specific names
rubrics_metrics.description: In every branch of moral action employing Practical Wisdom there will be general principles and their application; in some branches particular names are appropriated (e.g., legislation for the general principles of civil government, government for administering particular functions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that practical reasoning manifests differently across domains (legislation, domestic management, administration) though the faculty is the same.
